title: Could Your School Lose Internet? A Big Program That Pays for It Is in Danger
summary: Imagine walking into school and finding out the internet is gone. No online quizzes, no digital textbooks, no streaming videos for class. That could happen if a program called E-Rate gets cut. E-Rate is a government program that helps schools and libraries pay for internet at a discount. It started in the 1990s, when only 14% of schools had internet. Now, almost 100% do, thanks in part to E-Rate. But now, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) is reviewing the program, and some people are worried it might shrink or disappear. David Thurston works with technology for 33 school districts in San Bernardino County, California—a huge area with mountains, deserts, and cities. He says E-Rate pays for tens of thousands of dollars in internet bills every month. "There's no doing without," he says. If the money goes away, schools would have to find it somewhere else. The FCC's chairman, Brendan Carr, says one reason for the review is to limit kids' screen time. He points to research that too much screen time can be bad for children. Some states, like Alabama and Utah, have already passed laws to reduce screen time in schools. But many experts say cutting internet funding isn't the right way to solve that problem. "We believe there are ways of strengthening school policies to promote more limited and privacy-protecting use of EdTech without taking away critical E-Rate funding," said Josh Golin from Fairplay, a group that focuses on digital safety for kids. Schools use the internet for a lot more than just screens. They track attendance, plan bus routes, and give state tests online. In fact, 48 states now have online exams. Bob Bocher from the American Library Association says the FCC probably can't kill E-Rate completely because it's written into a law from 1996. But they could make it so complicated that schools and libraries give up trying to use it. That would be a big problem for millions of students.
why_it_matters: If your school couldn’t afford internet, you might not be able to use online textbooks, take state tests, or do research for projects—making school much harder for everyone.

background_read: The E-Rate program was created by the Telecommunications Act of 1996, a law that also helped make the internet available to more people. At that time, most schools had no internet at all.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC)—the government agency that oversees phone, TV, and internet rules—runs E-Rate. Today, nearly 100% of U.S. schools are connected, partly because of this program.
Libraries also benefit: many people who don’t have home internet rely on library computers to do homework, apply for jobs, or learn new skills.
Article_Structure: WHO: David Thurston (technology director), FCC chairman Brendan Carr, digital safety advocate Josh Golin, library expert Bob Bocher
WHAT: The FCC is reviewing the E-Rate program that helps schools afford internet, and many worry it could be cut or made too complicated to use
WHERE: Across the United States, with an example from San Bernardino County, California
WHY: Some officials want to reduce kids’ screen time, but educators say the internet is vital for online tests, attendance, bus routes, and digital learning

perspectives.description: Some people, including the FCC chairman, believe cutting internet funding would force schools to limit screens, helping kids focus more on physical activity and face‑to‑face learning.

Technology directors like David Thurston say schools cannot operate without internet—losing E-Rate would mean finding huge amounts of money somewhere else, or students would lose essential digital tools.

Groups like Fairplay argue that limiting screen time is important, but gutting E-Rate isn't the right solution; better policies on how technology is used in classrooms would protect kids without taking away internet access.
